summary: Describes a mechanism to carry IPv4 packets across an IPv6 network by encapsulation. It also describes a generic way to map between IPv6 addresses and IPv4 addresses and ports.

eli5.summary: Putting an old-style letter inside a new-style envelope, with a formula to know where it goes.

questions: mapping of address and port encapsulation
how does map-e share ipv4 addresses
subtitle: Carry IPv4 across an IPv6 network by encapsulation, with addresses and ports worked out from a formula instead of a lookup table.

tldr.problem: Networks moving to IPv6 still need to deliver IPv4 service, often with several customers sharing one IPv4 address, and the provider would prefer not to keep per-customer or per-flow state.
tldr.mechanism: MAP-E has the customer edge router run NAPT44 within an assigned port set and encapsulate IPv4 in IPv6, while mapping rules let any MAP node derive a customer's IPv4 address, port set and IPv6 address from the customer's IPv6 prefix.
tldr.outcome: Border relays are stateless and CEs can reach each other directly in mesh mode, but shared addresses bring a restricted port set, fragmentation caveats and port-guessing risks.

facts.label: Sharing ratio
facts.value: 2^k, where k is the PSID length

facts.label: Interface identifier layout
facts.value: 16 bits zero, 32 bits IPv4, 16 bits PSID

today: RFC 7597 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The companion RFC 7596 (Lightweight 4over6), published the same month, takes a binding-table approach and cites MAP-E as offering similar capabilities.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Earlier IPv6-over-IPv4 transition mechanisms such as automatic tunneling, 6over4, 6to4, ISATAP and 6rd embed an IPv4 address in an IPv6 address, so a tunnel endpoint can be calculated rather than looked up. The RFC notes that in later phases of the move to IPv6, IPv6-only networks will be common but some IPv4 will remain.

RFC 7597 applies the same idea in the opposite direction. It describes a generic mapping between IPv4 and IPv6 plus a mechanism for encapsulating IPv4 in IPv6. It must be able to provision an IPv4 prefix, an IPv4 address or a shared IPv4 address, and to map algorithmically between those and an IPv6 address. It supports both mesh and hub-and-spoke topologies, including mappings with full independence between IPv6 and IPv4 addresses. Only IPv4 unicast is covered.

The stateless approach corresponds to the Address plus Port architecture of RFC 6346; the stateful counterpart is Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333). DHCPv6 options to provision MAP are in RFC 7598.
sections.eli5: Old IPv4 mail still has to get delivered even though the roads are now IPv6. MAP-E wraps the old mail in IPv6 packaging and uses a simple rule to know where to send it.

sections.title: Architecture: CE, Border Relay and MAP Domain
sections.content:
A MAP domain is a set of MAP Customer Edge (CE) devices and Border Relays (BRs) on the same virtual link. The CE usually serves a residential site with a private IPv4 network. The BR is a provider-managed router at the domain edge with an IPv6 interface and an IPv4 interface to the native IPv4 network.

The CE uses an ordinary NAPT44 with extra support for restricting transport ports, ICMP identifiers and fragment identifiers to its assigned port set. For outbound packets the CE NAPT MUST translate transport identifiers so they fall within the CE's port range. The NAPT feeds a MAP-aware forwarding function that encapsulates IPv4 in IPv6 using the mode in RFC 2473.

A shared IPv4 address is used only as the outside address of the CE's NAPT, and MUST NOT be used to identify an interface. With a full IPv4 address or a prefix, the CE can use it normally and the NAPT does not have to restrict ports.
sections.eli5: Each home has a gateway that sorts its mail into the right numbered mailbox range and packs it in an IPv6 envelope. A relay at the edge of the provider's network takes the envelopes to and from the old IPv4 world.

sections.title: Mapping Rules
sections.content:
Every MAP node is provisioned with a Basic Mapping Rule (BMR), which is mandatory. It is matched to the node's End-user IPv6 prefix by longest match against the Rule IPv6 prefix, and is used to derive the node's IPv4 prefix, address or shared address and its PSID. An optional Forwarding Mapping Rule (FMR) maps a destination IPv4 address and port to the End-user IPv6 address that can reach it, which enables direct CE-to-CE traffic in mesh mode. In hub-and-spoke mode there are no FMRs and all traffic goes to the BR. All CEs MUST support both rule types.

Both rule types share three parameters: the Rule IPv6 prefix, the Rule IPv4 prefix and the Rule EA-bit length. The EA (embedded address) bits sit in the IPv6 address right after the Rule IPv6 prefix and carry part or all of the IPv4 address and, for shared addresses, a PSID. Their length can be 0 to 48. A length of 0 means all IPv4 information comes from the rule or from provisioning, not from the IPv6 prefix.

Using r for the Rule IPv4 prefix length and o for the EA-bit length, the outcome depends on o + r:

  • Less than 32: an IPv4 prefix is assigned.
  • Exactly 32: a full IPv4 address is assigned.
  • More than 32: a shared IPv4 address is assigned, and the PSID has length o minus the number of suffix bits p.

The sum of the Rule IPv6 prefix length and the EA-bit length MUST be no more than the End-user IPv6 prefix length. Traffic whose destination matches no Rule IPv4 prefix is sent to the BR, encapsulated with the BR's configured IPv6 address as destination. When MAP is enabled, a typical CE installs a default IPv4 route to the BR.
sections.eli5: The rule is like a street-numbering recipe. Given a house's long IPv6 address, the recipe tells you its IPv4 number and which door numbers it owns, so nobody has to keep a big address book.

sections.title: The MAP IPv6 Address and Interface Identifier
sections.content:
The MAP IPv6 address is the End-user IPv6 prefix, then the MAP subnet identifier (the first subnet, with the s bits set to zero) if the prefix is shorter than 64 bits, then the interface identifier. It MUST be assigned to an interface of the MAP node and terminates all MAP traffic to and from that node.

The interface identifier has 16 zero bits, then the 32-bit IPv4 address, then a 16-bit PSID. For an IPv4 prefix, the address field is right-padded with zeros to 32 bits. The PSID is left-padded with zeros to 16 bits, and is zero for a prefix or a full address. If the End-user prefix is longer than 64 bits, the prefix overwrites the most significant parts of the interface identifier.
sections.eli5: The last half of the IPv6 address is built to hold the IPv4 address and the door-number range, so anyone can read them straight off the address.

sections.title: The Port-Mapping Algorithm
sections.content:
When an IPv4 address is shared, each CE gets a separate part of the port space called a port set, identified by a PSID. The algorithm uses an infix layout of the 16-bit port number made of three fields: A (a bits), the PSID (k bits) and j (m bits). A CE therefore gets a series of contiguous ranges spaced at regular intervals across the whole port range.

  • a is the offset, 6 by default, which excludes the system ports 0-1023. A MUST be larger than 0, and a MUST be the same for every CE sharing an address. Smaller values exclude a larger initial range; a = 4 excludes ports 0-4095.
  • k is the PSID length and MUST also be the same for every CE sharing the address. The sharing ratio is 2^k.
  • m sets the number of contiguous ports, 2^m.

Appendix B explains the design goals: non-overlapping port sets, a PSID that can be embedded in the IPv6 prefix, a mapping that is reversible, and nearly equal port counts per CE. It names the approach the Generalized Modulus Algorithm, in which a port is P = (R * M) * i + M * PSID + j for sharing ratio R and maximum contiguous ports M, and the PSID of a port is trunc((P modulo (R * M)) / M).
sections.eli5: Imagine a long row of numbered lockers shared by many families. Each family gets a few lockers in a row, repeated at regular spots all along the row, so no two families ever share a locker.

sections.title: Forwarding, ICMP and Fragmentation
sections.content:
For a shared address, the CE first does NAT44, so the packet carries the source IPv4 address and transport identifiers from its MAP parameters. It then encapsulates, and the IPv6 source and destination are derived from the mapping rules. A CE receiving an IPv6 packet to its MAP address decapsulates it and passes it to NAT44. A BR picks the best matching rule by longest match on the IPv6 source address and checks the destination against its configured BR address.

To prevent IPv4 spoofing, every MAP node MUST extract the allowed IPv4 address and PSID from the packet's IPv6 source using the matching rule, then check the inner IPv4 source address and port. If they fall outside that range, the packet MUST be silently discarded and a counter incremented. These checks are not done when the IPv6 source is the BR's address.

For ICMP, the CE's NAT44 MUST follow RFC 5508 and MUST rewrite an ICMP Identifier to a value from the port set. Encapsulation typically adds 40 bytes, so the RFC strongly recommends managing the MTU so no fragmentation occurs inside the domain. A BR using an anycast source address SHOULD NOT by default use Path MTU Discovery across the domain. A MAP node receiving fragmented IPv4 from outside has to reassemble before sending it on, and fragments sent outward by CEs sharing an address may collide on the 16-bit fragment identifier.
sections.eli5: Every gateway checks that the return address on an envelope matches the IPv4 address and door numbers inside, so nobody can pretend to be someone else. The envelope makes the letter bigger, so the network should be set up so letters need not be chopped up.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Appendix A works an example. The End-user IPv6 prefix is 2001:db8:0012:3400::/56 and the BMR is Rule IPv6 prefix 2001:db8:0000::/40, Rule IPv4 prefix 192.0.2.0/24, EA-bit length 16. The IPv4 suffix is 8 bits and the PSID length is 8, a sharing ratio of 256.

From this the node derives the IPv4 address 192.0.2.18, the PSID 0x34, and the available ports 1232-1235, 2256-2259 and so on up to 64720-64723 (63 ranges). The CE's MAP IPv6 address is 2001:db8:0012:3400:0000:c000:0212:0034.

In the BR example with BR address 2001:db8:ffff::1, a packet to 192.0.2.18 port 1232 is encapsulated to that CE address. In the reverse direction, a host behind the CE talking to 1.2.3.4 has its packets sent from the CE's MAP address to the BR.
sections.eli5: The example walks through the recipe with real numbers: from one long IPv6 address it works out the IPv4 address, the door-number range, and the full address of the router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists four concerns. With the IPv4/IPv6 source consistency checks, MAP introduces no new spoofing opportunity beyond those already in IPv6. Where IPv4 addresses are shared, reassembly of IPv4 datagrams may be needed, which opens a DoS opportunity common to address sharing in general. The RFC says the best protection is to accelerate IPv6 deployment.

Routing loop attacks known from some automatic tunneling scenarios cannot occur, because each BR checks that the IPv6 source of a received packet is a CE address based on the Forwarding Mapping Rule.

A restricted port set makes it easier for an attacker who is not subject to ingress filtering to guess ports and inject spoofed packets into connections. Native IPv6 with no port restriction is preferable. To reduce the risk, the CE's NAT44 filtering SHOULD be Address-Dependent Filtering from RFC 4787, and CEs SHOULD use a DNS transport proxy and source DNS traffic from IPv6 interfaces not assigned to MAP. General address-sharing issues are in RFC 6269.
sections.eli5: Because each home has fewer door numbers, a bad guy can guess them more easily. So the gateways are told to be pickier about which replies they let in, and to use plain IPv6 when they can.
